Gibeonites
GIB-ee-uh-nytes
proper noun (the people of Gibeon)
From Gibeon, a Hivite city of Canaan; the people who deceived Joshua into a covenant of peace and became hewers of wood and drawers of water for the sanctuary.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Gibeonites were the inhabitants of Gibeon, a Hivite city of Canaan, who, hearing of Israel's victories at Jericho and Ai and knowing they were marked for destruction, saved themselves by a cunning deception. They came to Joshua in worn-out clothes and with mouldy bread, claiming to be travellers from a far country, and so obtained a covenant of peace. The princes of the congregation sware unto them by the LORD; and when the deceit was discovered three days later, Israel would not break the oath, for it had been sworn in the name of the LORD. Joshua made the Gibeonites hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD—a servitude, yet a place within Israel and near the worship of God. Generations later, when Saul in his zeal slew the Gibeonites in breach of that ancient oath, a three-year famine fell upon David's land, for the LORD held the covenant binding still. The dictionary marks the Gibeonites for two abiding lessons. First, the sanctity of a sworn oath: Israel kept faith even with those who had deceived them, because the oath was taken in the LORD's name, and God avenged its later breach. Second, the mercy that gathers the outsider: a Canaanite people doomed to destruction found life and a place near the altar, a foretoken of the Gentiles brought nigh—though by deceit they came, the grace of God made even hewers of wood servants of His house.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Hivites of Gibeon who deceived Joshua into a covenant of peace and became hewers of wood for the sanctuary; Israel kept the oath sworn in the LORD's name, and avenged Saul's later breach of it with famine (Joshua 9; 2 Samuel 21:1).

expand to see more

GIBEONITES, proper noun. The Hivite inhabitants of Gibeon in Canaan.

They deceived Joshua, feigning to be from a far country, to obtain a covenant (Joshua 9:3-15).

Israel kept the oath though deceived, for it was sworn in the name of the LORD.

They were made hewers of wood and drawers of water for the altar (Joshua 9:27).

Saul's later breach of the oath brought a three-year famine on David's land (2 Samuel 21:1).

📖 Key Scripture

Jos 9:3 — "And when the inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done unto Jericho and to Ai,"

Jos 9:15 — "And Joshua made peace with them, and made a league with them, to let them live: and the princes of the congregation sware unto them."

Jos 9:27 — "And Joshua made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD, even unto this day, in the place which he should choose."

2 Sa 21:1 — "Then there was a famine in the days of David three years, year after year; and David enquired of the LORD. And the LORD answered, It is for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the modern lightness toward sworn oaths, which Scripture treats as binding even when obtained by deceit and avenged when broken.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the binding sanctity of a sworn oath. Israel had been deceived into the covenant with Gibeon, and might have argued the oath void for fraud; yet because it was sworn in the name of the LORD, they held it inviolable, and centuries later God Himself avenged its breach with famine. The modern age treats vows and contracts as lightly broken when inconvenient. The dictionary recovers the biblical weight: he that sweareth to his own hurt and changeth not (Psalm 15:4) honours the God in whose name he swore, and the LORD requires the keeping of oaths even toward those who wronged us.

The Gibeonites also display the reach of God's mercy. A Canaanite people doomed to destruction found life and a settled place near the altar of the LORD—hewers of wood and drawers of water, yet within Israel and serving the worship of God. The dictionary reads this, with sober care not to commend the deceit, as a foretoken of the Gentiles brought nigh: the outsider, even the enemy, gathered into the household of God. The grace that spared Gibeon prefigures the grace that, in Christ, makes those who were far off to be made nigh, and aliens to become servants in the house of the Lord.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Gibeon (Hebrew Giv'on, “hill city”), a Hivite city north of Jerusalem; its people a remnant of the Canaanites spared by the oath of the princes.

expand to see more

Giv'on, Hebrew, “hill city,” the chief Hivite town.

The Hivites, one of the Canaanite nations marked for the herem.

“Hewers of wood and drawers of water” (Joshua 9:27), their appointed servitude.

The “league” (Hebrew berith, covenant) sworn by the princes in the LORD's name.

The tabernacle later stood at Gibeon in the days of David and Solomon.

Usage

"The pastor preached the Gibeonites to teach the binding sanctity of an oath sworn in the LORD's name."

"He noted that God avenged Saul's breach of the ancient covenant with a three-year famine."

"She saw in the spared Canaanites a foretoken of the Gentiles gathered near the altar of God."
